newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA proposes requiring dioxin disclosure.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA proposes requiring dioxin disclosure.

text.p: The Environmental Protection Agency Monday proposed adding dioxin -- a highly toxic byproduct of some industrial processes -- to the list of chemicals whose release industries must disclose under a community-right-to-know programme.
Siding with environmental groups, the agency said the agency would propose making industries report their emissions of dioxin and 27 dioxin-like compounds that accumulate in body tissues.

But in its proposal, the EPA acknowledged that industries probably will not actually have to report their dioxin emissions unless the agency also lowers the threshold on levels of emissions that must be disclosed.
Dioxin, toxic in tiny amounts, is emitted in lower concentrations that other substances that industries currently must report on in the Toxic Release Inventory programme.
The EPA said it would consider lowering threshold levels for dioxin later, and asked for public comment on threshold levls.
"We think it's great that they're adding dioxin, but there are still a lot of loopholes," Carolyn Hartmann, of the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, said.
"Since it is an unintentional byproduct, it doesn't fall under current reporting requirements. It also doesn't hit the 10,000-pound threshold, so this is just a preliminary step," Hartmann said.
Industries have complained that the Toxic Inventory Release programme is intrusive and may force manufacturers to reveal proprietary information.
Dioxin is a waste byproduct of combustion or incineration involving chlorine. It is a known carcinogen and may be more dangerous as a disrupter of endocrine and nervous systems, according to experts.

"Although dioxin is not intentionally produced, it is coincidentally manufactured in several industrial processes commonly used in the combustion and incineration of waste, steel production, pulp and paper manufacturing, and oil refining, among other operations," the EPA said in a statement.
The comment period on the proposal ends July 6, and a final decision on whether to include dioxin "will be made when EPA finalises a lower numeric reporting threshold for dioxin," the agency said.
